rents into to-day's stock market were ex-
ceedingly confusing and irregular and
the day's contest between speculative
forces was by no means conclusive. A
very large amount of liquidation was
brought about and there were periods
of acute and general weakness. Some of
the recently prominent stocks in the ad-
vance suffered material setbacks. On
the other hand there were stocks whose
strength was constant in varying de-
gree throughout the session. The selling
movement showed symptoms of having
largely expended itself during the course

bull interests and the market rallied
throughout from the midday low level.

there were indications that the perso-
nality of the leaders of the speculation had
also undergone some change. The
brokers who were the largest sellers in
the railroad list, were very heavy buyers
of some of the steel stocks and it was ev-
ident that an attempt was to be made to
conduct a double campaign in the mar-

roads and on the bull side in the steel

we have every right to presuppose
this, reason would then be impotent
to show us by what means we might
correct the error, make atonement, and
regain the happiness which by that act
was forever forfeited. Moreover, rea-
son itself will tell every sane man that
during this present life it can never
acquire the knowledge of all truth.
The time, the application, the oppor-
tunity as well as the inclination are
wanting in the vast majority of men
to study and reason out even those
few most important truths, upon the
knowledge of which depends the at-
tainment of our end. These truths
may not be beyond our natural capa-
city. If we would consider man
with Plato's genius and Aristotle's sol-
idity, perchance such one would ob-
tain to this knowledge after years of
serious thought, for these truths are
the proper and proportionate object of
the intellect. But where, I pray you,
is this combination of Aristotle and
Plato to be found? How many such
are there? It is most important that
we take this question into considera-
tion here, for we speak not of few,
but of humanity at large. It is a ques-
tion of salvation for the human race.
The answer given most clearly and
enthusiastically by the history of the
past as well as by the observation of
every day is that beyond any doubt
few, if any, could be found or could be
placed in such favorable circumstances
that their reason, unaided by a single
extraordinary help from on high,
would ever discover all those truths
which pertain to the essence of reli-
gion, and without which they could
never attain to God—their end. These
truths in themselves are most sublime;
in knowing God consists the highest
grade of human knowledge. How few
are apt to reach it! How few can
ever hope to acquire more than a cur-
sory knowledge of material things,
while the immaterial and spiritual fur-
ther exceed their grasp. And of those who
may have the mental acumen, how
few have the inclination, the energy
of purpose, to apply themselves as
assiduously to the study of abstract
truths? Even granting that these con-
ditions be fulfilled, there still remains
another which is a difficulty insur-
mountable. These truths, as has been
said, are high and difficult for reason
to attain. They require all man's in-
tellectual power, and as necessary
consequence they demand a long time
of serious and constant application.

Just before W. C. Spalding left Washington last evening for South Carolina he was shown a copy of an alleged letter from Andrew Freedman's New York attorney making certain deductions from Mr. Spalding's circular letter of Dec. 8, addressed to the National League clubs, Mr. Spalding said:

"Mr. Freedman's attorney is at perfect liberty to make any deductions from that letter he pleases, but it speaks for itself. The quotation that this New York attorney makes from my letter is as misleading as everything else Mr. Freedman has done since the baseball controversy began.

An Omitted introduction.

"...If he had preceded his quotation with the words pending the decision of the court, he would have shown a stronger disposition to quote my letter correctly.

"On December 1A was informed by committee of the National League that I had been unanimously elected president of that organization on that date. Col. John R. Rogers, a prominent attorney of Philadelphia, has assured me that that election was regular and legal; a similar opinion has been expressed by my personal attorney, Alfred W. Kiddie, of New York.

"I believe I am the legally elected president of the National League, and as I consider opinions as quoted above quite as good as the opinion of Mr. Freedman's attorney, I shall continue to believe myself the legally elected president of the National League until some court of competent jurisdiction shall decide otherwise.

Awaits the Decision

"Pending this final decision, and in accordance with an order of the Supreme Court of New York, I am temporarily restrained from acting as president-secretary-treasurer of the National League, and I must bow to the majesty of the law and comply with the court's order. I am not a lawyer, and do not pretend to the intricacies of court procedure, but have instructed my attorney to do whatever in his judgment he may deem necessary to make a proper answer at the proper time to any and all charges that may be preferred by Mr. Freedman and those who, for personal reasons, seem to deem it necessary to continue their association with him in these legal proceedings.

Insists on a Trial.

"I have instructed my attorney to insist that the case be brought to a trial, and not permitted to be dismissed until a final decision has been reached. Mr. Freedman's attorney's contention that the issuance of a temporary injunction upon the hearing only of Mr. Freedman's side of the case settles the matter in Mr. Freedman's favor is too ridiculous to treat seriously, and was given out probably for the purpose of throwing dust in the eyes of the baseball public to befog the real issue, and also to stampede the four clubs that are responsible for my election.

"It is rather amusing that Mr. Freedman, who has until recently been in the habit of deciding all baseball questions, should now find it necessary to employ an attorney to make deductions from an ordinary business correspondence. All of this shows that Mr. Freedman realizes he is in the quicksand, and is ready to grasp anything to save himself.

Some other Deductions.

"As Mr. Freedman has seen fit to make deductions through his attorney as to my actions and motives, it may not seem out of place for me to make some deductions as to his recent actions and motives. Having publicly read Mr. Freedman out of the National League baseball political party, I construe these recent court proceedings simply to mean that he recognizes that he is out and through the aid of a court is trying to get back again; and also by these proceedings to create sort of toboggan slide to make his baseball fall more gradual and less abrupt.

Trying to Bulldoze.

"I also construe these recent deductions made by Mr. Freedman's attorney as simply calculated to bulldoze and frighten the league clubs that are responsible for my election into further submission to Mr. Freedman's dictatorial rule-or-ruin policy that has characterized his handling of baseball affairs since he has been connected with the game. It looks to me as if Mr. Freedman has just discovered that those court proceedings have entangled him and those associated with him in such a way that he is now trying to find some way to extricate himself, but he must do this without my assistance.

"I look upon these court proceedings as simply another evidence of Mr. Freedman's baseball methods, and it is up to him to disentangle himself from these legal complications that he has instituted as best he can. It is again up to Mr. Freedman to make another move.

To Aid the Game.

"As I am temporarily restrained from taking up my official league duties pending the decision of the court, I will continue along in the even tenor of my way and try to create new conditions that will tend to place professional baseball upon much better basis than it has been since Mr. Freedman's advent into the game."

On the shores of the Mediterranean there lies between France and Italy the little kingdom of Monaco. It numbers fewer inhabitants than a large village in all Europe, and is in extent so contracted as not to boast more than double that number of acres. But, on the other hand, it has a rural prince, who possesses a palace, a court, ministers, bishops, generals and an army. Not, to be sure, large army—sixty men—still an army; nor is the revenue large. Duties are, indeed, as elsewhere, imposed upon wine, alcohol and tobacco; but although the people conscientiously drink and smoke there are not enough of them, and the princeling would certainly be unable to feed his courtiers and himself had he not the special resource of a gambling house.


There people lose or gain, as the case may be, but the keeper always profits, and, therefore, pays heavy dues to the princeling. He can well afford to do so as his establishment is in Europe unique. Similar places formerly existed in some of the German principalities; but years ago on account of frequent catastrophes they were suppressed. A player carried away by excitement, would lose all his own money, and sometimes even that of others, and then commit suicide. So the Germans forbade their little princes to keep gambling houses, but no one could forbid the potentate of Monaco and that is why he has a monopoly.


Therefore all the lovers of trente et quarante rush to his kingdom, and for toil does not enrich, says the Russian proverb. The princeling knows that the spring from which he drains is impure, but what can he do? It would not be more honest to increase his income by raising the duties on alcohol and tobacco; a man must live! So the princeling lives in peace, makes money, and like a real sovereign lives surrounded by courtly ceremonial. He rewards, punishes, reviews his troops, holds councils and promulgates laws, just like other rulers, only on a smaller scale.


Now, some years since a serious event took place in the kingdom. A murder was committed. The inhabitants of Monaco are peaceable folk, and nothing of the sort had ever before taken place among them. The judges met, and, as was proper, set about judging. All was lawyer, jury, long and conscientious debates. Then, in accordance with the law, they condemned the assassin to death. So far, so good. The sentence was submitted to the princeling and after his ratification all that remained to be done was to execute it. But an impediment presented itself. The country possessed neither guillotine nor executioner.


After mature consideration it was decided that to obtain the loan of a master cutter-off of heads, together with his apparatus, the French government should be addressed, and that at the same time inquiry as to the cost of the move should be made. Eight days later the answer was received. The French government consented to send the guillotine and the executioner. As to the expenses, they would amount to 10,000 francs.


The matter was referred to the princeling. His majesty thought the assassin was not worth the price. Sixteen thousand francs for the neck of this rascal! No, indeed, it would in that case be necessary to increase by francs yearly the taxes of each citizen. The people might resist.


A council was held and it was decided to address the same request to the King of Italy. France is a republic, and republics do not respect Caesars, but the King of Italy, a brother, might be less extortionate. The reply was immediate. One can scarcely step anywhere on the little mid-Pacific island of Lay San without treading on a bird or birds nest, and countless thousands of albatrosses breed here in great colonies. Of the albatrosses on Lay San there are two kinds-the brown and the white, says writer in Pear sons Magazine. The two species, of which the white are far the common CT, always keep apart from each oth- CT, the dark albatrosses breeding away from the others on the south side of the island. The brown birds are dark, sooty color all over. The beautiful white albatrosses are pure white beneath, with blackish brown wings and white heads, having only 8 little black patch in front of the eyes. They measure over 30 inches in length, with wings each Is inches long, bill four inches and a claw four inches. Two albino albatrosses-pure white all over-have been seen, but were evil dently quite exceptional. The alba tross' nest is merely a lump of earth, with hole in the middle. Each moth CT bird lays but one egg, and this is placed in the hole, point downward. The young birds, as they air them selves on the beach, are fed by both loving parents. Their diet is fish. The parent bird brings home the fish in his capacious maw. At meal times the offspring puts his little beak cross- wise into his parents, who then clev- erly produces the fish from his nat ural fish basket.

 It is curious that though in many places on Lay-San alba atrosses stand a $ closely together as there is room for the neighboring French Frigate shoals. Then they shake hands and snap their bills with marvellous rapidity, walking around each other for 15 minutes at a time.

me—"


"He has not been kind to me," vehemently. "He said he did not know where
you were!"


"I made him promise that when
I knew you were returning. Somehow I
felt—I have always felt—you were coming
back. But now you must go away again.
You must forget me. I will not let my
blindness be a burden and a barrier to
you."


"You are thinner, paler than of old,
Margaret, but sweeter—for your sadness
to me!"


"I have suffered," she said simply.
"Now go!"


Instead he put firm, professional fingers
on her eyes—forced her to let him look
long and steadily. A sound like a sob,
still joyful sound, broke from him.


"I can cure you, Margaret!" His voice
was hoarse with exultation. "Thank
God for that. I can cure you!"


Just then Dr. Griscom came in. Car-
nivert gave his message. The men went
away.


"Fate brought you together after all,"
Griscom said. "You do not blame me?"


"You could not break your word, but
should not have given such a promise."


"How could I tell you loved her still
after all these years?"


"I thought you were my friend. The
intuition of a friend is definite as divine.
Do you think it is in my nature to love
lightly—to forget?"


"I know it is not. I ask your pardon."


"Here we are at the house; I shall
wait to hear how the dear little lad is."


Griscom took the stairs three at a
time. "Better!" he cried, coming down,
radiant. "At least he is in no danger.
His mother was unnecessarily alarmed.
It is only tonsilitis. He will be about
in a few days."


"That is fine! Now I must be selfish
for a few minutes. Come into the libra-

comrade. "Harry," he said, "I can cure
Margaret!"


"Eustace!" cried Griscom. "Are you
sure? For God's sake, don't deceive
yourself!"


"I have examined her eyes. I am posi-
tive. The operation will be similar to
that which brought me the success I had
fought so long to win."


The weeks that followed were weeks
of eager hope, of confident anticipation,
of rapturous conviction. Doubt, despair—
these had no place in the sanguine mind
of the great oculist.


It came—the all eventful day. Then
there was the enforced period of seclu-
sion, of waiting. But when the hour ar-
rived when Carnivert was to remove the
bandages from the long unseeing eyes of
Margaret Chester, his hand trembled for
the first time.


"Look!" he commanded in straining
whisper. "Look, beloved." Her voice
rang out, thrilling those who heard. "I
can see. I can see. Eustace, Eustace!"
Oh, the ecstasy of that cry! "I can see
you!"


Then he had caught her in his arms.
Her head was on his shoulder, her happy
face crushed against his breast.


"Old fellow," Griscom said reverently,
"there is something I must tell you now.
After that parting between you and Mar-
garet she transferred to you all the prop-
erty she personally possessed. It was an
legacy to her from an aunt. That is the
money which you spoke of as having
come to you mysteriously. Her lawyers
were bound to silence. Without that
gift of exquisite generosity you could
never have gone abroad, studied, fulfilled
your dreams of success, attained your
present eminence!"


"Nor given Margaret back her sight,"
Dr. Griscom's wife said softly.
Margaret was smiling through joyful
tears. And her lover, in silence more
eloquent than any speech, looked down
upon her.—St. Louis Republic.

Wallace Rathburn, who fled the place last week Wednesday night to escape arrest for attempting the rape of Hazel, a ten-year-old daughter of Charles Stockwell, was captured in Canaan, N. H. It became known to the officers that he had formerly worked there and notice was sent to the authorities to watch for him. Word was received Monday that he was held a prisoner and would be delivered at White River Junction, he being willing to come without requisition. Rathburn was taken to Chelsea Tuesday afternoon by Officer Parish on an information filed by the state's attorney. He will be tried at the present term of county court. He is 26 years of age, has a wife and one small child. His wife was helped by the overseer of the poor to reach her sister's home in South Pomfret, her child accompanying her.

Minneapolis, Times: Ida and Hans P. Britzka of North Dakota will today ask the district court to give them possession of their 2-year-old boy, Alex.

F. L. Mcclellan, 2016 Kenwood Park way, president of the Mcclellan Paper company, and his wife, will resist the granting of the motion, because they want to adopt the baby and have already taken steps to that end.

The wife and husband wanted a baby, Mr. Shattuck wanted a grandchild, but none came to bless the household. So last Christmas the family decided to find a homeless baby boy and adopt him—a kind of Christmas present to the family.

Some time before Christmas a man at the Maternity hospital had noticed an advertisement from a small place in North Dakota, which stated there was a baby boy up there for whom a home was wanted. The advertisement was published by the aunt of the child.

The advertisement was answered, and the aunt was informed that the baby could find a place at the Maternity hospital, and it was likely that it would be only a short time before a good home would be found for him.

The baby was sent to the hospital by the aunt. Mr. Shattuck and the McClellans heard of the circumstances, inspected the baby, and were satisfied. He was brought to the home on Christmas morning, and the first steps toward his adoption taken.

On October 5 a petition for the adoption by Mcclellan was presented to Judge Elliott. Ida and Hans Britzka filed an objection, claiming that they are entitled to the possession of the child, being his parents. The case was continued today.

In fact, although he took his hunting clothes, and guns and ammunition with him, this latter is his real mission.

He will take dinner with the Britzkas, without letting them know who he is, and try to ascertain what has become of the "aunt" who placed the baby in the Maternity hospital and gave authority to the hospital to find a home for him.

Mr. Mcclellan will be back today in time to be present when the case is called up in the district court.

It was generally understood that the attitude of the great body towards the question of divorce would be brought up for final settlement; but at the very beginning, another question which has caused much agitation, and upon which the communicants, laity and clergy, are divided was brought before the body.

Bishop Morris, of Oregon, is responsible for bringing to the attention of the convention the question of ritualism. In an address before the body he denounced certain of its phases in language that might have come from a Methodist or a Presbyterian. It is the most difficult problem the church has to solve, and is as old as the idea of worship. There are many elements which go to make up opinions in this matter; temperament, training, prejudice and custom. At bottom it is a question of psychology, and that is the reason that the race has been so long and so positively divided on it.

The High Church and the Low Church have each had loyal adherents, and open rupture has been prevented by a charity and a policy which have prevented a clash in opinions. In short there has been spirit of concession and liberation, which has allowed individual churches considerable latitude.

There are those who claim that the canons are to be obeyed without question, as being of such authority that human judgment has no option but to set them aside; the customs which have prevailed from time immemorial are regarded as binding, just as in civil life we regard the common law. The Low Churchman, however, holds such a view as narrow and arbitrary, and believes that a ritual is established largely as a convenience in worship.

But ritualism, too, is defended on grounds of psychology and philosophy. Its supporters declare that human beings cannot approach the Infinite, save through the finite, and that symbolism is a necessary part of worship, since it enables the mind to form some concrete picture which fixes it upon lofty things, otherwise beyond the human grasp. We are told that customs, ancient and venerable, which have been employed for centuries, are so intimately associated with sacred things that to deny their exalted character is sacrilege, and tends to bring religious worship into contempt. Many analogies may be found to support this position. Even the members of those sects which have discarded the ritual admit to a degree the argument holds. It is deemed a rare religious privilege to look upon those scenes where the Master trod, even by those who hold that no material thing can be consecrated. On the other hand there is in some church feeling that the ceremony may of itself engage the attention, or the exclusion of that which it is intended to represent. In other words, the mind may go no further than the symbol, and become devoted to it.

The severe drought has been hard
on pastures, both on account of lack
of moisture and on account of over
stocking. The sod is killed out in
places, and weeds will come in. A
great deal of our natural pasture
land should not be broken except
when new seeding becomes abso-
lutely necessary, and the lifetime of
these pastures could be prolonged by
some attention right now. The best
way to control weeds is to crowd
them out, and there is no better plant
than timothy to do this until until
better pasture grasses can get new
foothold. In September, no matter
if the weather is dry, a grain drill,
with sharp hoes, should be run over
all thin patches in the pasture, dis
tributing one-fourth TO one-third of
bushel of timothy seed an acre in
connection with 200 pounds an acre of
high-grade acid phosphate. The
drill-hoes will put the thin sod so that
some of the seed will find fresh soil
for starting when the fall rains come,
and the trash of the old sod will fur
nish some winter protection to the
new plants. If some stable manure
can be spared for light top dressing
it will pay well in making sod that
will choke out the weeds. We expect
too much of our pastures, and help
them too little. If the bare spots were
given some seed in bad years, and
some fertilizers were added after
light scratching of the surface, weeds
would be kept under control, more
grass would be gotten, and the break
ing-plow need not be used so frequent
ly on land that needs the protection
of sod all the time. If we would
look upon pasture grasses as n crop,
and give them attention when most
needed, our labor would be rewarded
fully as well as it is when applied to
most titled crops.-Farm and Fireside.

dications of the commencement of this
trouble. Chronic catarrh is likely to
end in deafness.-Good Health.

"One of the most laughable scenes as ever witnessed during the representation of one of Shakespeare's tragedies," said a well-known theatrical manager to the writer, "happened to the late Tom Kelson when he was performing in northern New York town. The company was playing Julius Caesar and at the last moment it was found that the regular throne chair used in the late scene, and an old rustic chair, was hastily procured from the left of the theater and, after being covered with draping, was pressed into service. In the midst of the scene a large wasp's nest was discovered attached to this chair, and its inhabitants, becoming indignant at the disturbance they had suffered, began to swarm about the stage, seeking revenge upon the Romans in their low-necked and short-sleeved dresses. The wasps seemed to be particularly offended with Caesar, and it is doubtful if Caesar's death scene was ever acted with more hilarity, for at the moment he was being pierced by the conspirators' daggers the wasps were most industrious in their work.

"In the tent scene where Caesar appears to Brutus one might almost have doubted its being the real Caesar. It was the same in form and dress, but the face was no longer the same. For seven weeks I was a prisoner, while the police had charge of my apartments and would give me no news whatever. The lawyer employed said that we must let the law take its course—that is, we must wait until the officials of the law got ready to let me prove my innocence. If I couldn't prove that I was not accessory to the missing man's suicide, then it would go hard with me. There came a day at last when I was arraigned in court. It was not on the main charge, but on that of obstructing the law. I had simply asked the inspector what he expected to find in my apartments to show what had become of my missing friend. That was made out to be "obstructing," and I was fined a sum equal to about $40. The next day I was brought in on another charge. It was my duty under the law to have notified the police at once of Leon's disappearance, but had waited several days before doing so. Being derelict in my duty, I was fined $5. There was still a third charge. I had employed private detectives when I should have notified the regular police. This was holding the law in contempt. It was clearly within the province of the court to fine me for that, but as I was a stranger in France and had not been found guilty of any criminal offense, this charge would be overlooked. I was then given my liberty, with a warning to be more circumspect in the future. My attorney had not opened his mouth in my defense, but I had to pay him a fee of $50.

Upon being turned out of the courtroom I made my way to my apartments to find that Messerve had been home for three days, but that the police had prevented him from notifying me. He had left the rooms fully intending to make an end of himself but had encountered friends, drunk with them in the house and won something like $40,900. His friends had taken care of him until he was once more himself. He had scarcely related his adventures and listened to mine when the police came and arrested him, and two days later he was tried and convicted of the charge of raising a false and unnecessary alarm and causing the officers of the law unusual and unnecessary trouble. This was based upon the fact that he had not committed suicide, and he was fined $40. I do not know if the police would have brought further charges, but did not wait to give them a chance. Bidding my companion adieu, I packed up and crossed the channel and left them to work it out on those remaining behind. A few weeks later I heard that the notary was in trouble, but whether because he had notified Messerve of his misfortune or for breaking some other article of the code, I could not learn.

Our Wares Make Inroads in Markets Of England.

English discussion of the American commercial invasion continues to grow more pointed and frank, says S. C. McFarland, consul at Nottingham in Consular Reports. Hardly an issue of the leading English papers appears without reference to American competition; for two years the tone of such articles has become serious, and economic writers are kept busy attempting to find acceptable explanations for American success. Leicester, in this consular district, is the seat of two great industries—the manufacture of boots and shoes and of hosiery (including underwear). A few days ago large quantities of boots and shoes were exported to the United States. Now, not only are there no exports, but enterprising American firms have actually opened retail stores there, while much of the machinery used is of American make. Hosiery exports a few years ago were very large. They are now comparatively small, and as shown in previous reports, are constantly declining in volume, and, to cap the climax, American goods are actually selling at retail in this market. As this is the very home of the British industry, it is not astonishing that such fact should come as shock to natural British pride, and that its importance, as disclosing the general trend of trade, should be minimized, and as rule, made light of. The leading trade organ, the Hosiery Trade Journal of Leicester, attempts in the following suggestive article in its current number to bring the more serious phases of the matter to the attention of its readers:

The report from the British consul at Philadelphia strengthens the fact that America is making fast strides in the manufacture of hosiery of all kinds, and that in the near future American goods will be met in many markets where same have been up to the present unknown. As such advancement takes place, so will decrease the importation by that country of hosiery goods, and those countries which have in the past supplied America with hosiery will have to find other markets. This is no surmise, for at the present time the exports of hosiery from both Germany and England are nothing like what they were in years past, and, as stated, have the tendency to still further decrease.

The corn, forever reaching up,
With growing ear and tasseled top,
To sun, or cloud, or cooling drop,
It bows down, and yields its golden prize,

In every zephyr's breath did sway,
In dewy morn or twilight gray,
All ripened, to the sickle keen
Surrenders, and is gathered in
To fill to overflow the bin.

The corn is in the storehouse fast.

So that I may, when life is done,
Be gathered in the harvest morn,
A fully ripened shock of corn!
And when, my little day complete,
I lie before the Reaper's feet,
May I be found among the wheat!

good stories of Gen. Grant when he
was a lieutenant in the Mexican war.
One is the mule story. He tried a de-
tail of men and many ropes, but the
mule got the better of the experiment.
Then his happened:


Returning, he gave orders to take
the next victim to a large rock. 1t was
backed as closely to the obstruction as
possible without actually touching it.
Half a dozen men were told to hold the
brute by the head, ears n neck, and
on no account to let it advance from
the rock. Then a man was told to clap
a harness on quickly. AS soon as the
buckles began to fasten the mule be-
came restless. Pretty soon it made a
sudden lunge and succeeded in getting
four feet away from the rock, and then
the fun began. His heels cracked
against the rock savagely for a short
time. 1t was a new experience, and,
apparently, a painful one, for the bat
tered hind feet were lifted again and
again, but very gently, and only one at
a time, while it's head shook and it's
ears Topped. That mule was cured,
and the problem was solved. The de-
tail returned to camp late that evening,
having accomplished it's mission-tak-
ing the kick out of a drove Of as I'M
manageable mules as ever hauled pork
and bareback.

A Washington, Nov. 25.-The trial of Mrs.
Lola Ida Bonine for the murder of James
Seymour Ayres, Jr.. at the Kenmore
Hotel last May, began in real earnest to-
day. The preliminary details as to the
finding of the body, the location of the
furniture, ETC.. were all in with the con-
,clusion of the testimony of J. f. Drew,
the capitol policeman who was on the
stand when the court adjourned last
FRIDAY


Baker the man who saw Mrs. Bonine
descend the fire escape; Hopkins, who
roomed over Ayres' and raised the first
outcry; Miss Woolums, who roomed
under Ayres, and Miss Lawless and Miss
Minas, who roomed on each side of him,
testified today The two latter were re-
garded as star witnesses, but they testi-
fled to no facts not developed at the in
guest.


Drew testified that there was room
enough behind the door of Ayres' room
for a man to have been there while the
door was opened to admit another per-
son, a contention which the prosecution
deny, and also that there were empty
cartridges in the slop jar in Ayres' room
before the pistol with which the shoot
ing was done was emptied by OFFICER
Brady after the tragedy This would
tend to establish the theory of the de
fense that the pistol belonged to Ayres.
Mrs. Bonine, throughout the trial today
when witnesses described the cries,
groans and throat gurgling of the dying
man remained absolutely unmoved.


j. Frank Drew, the capitol policeman,
who was on the stand last Friday when
the court adjourned, resumed his testi-
mony. He swore that he had several
times seen the defendant come out of
Ayres' room. The last occasion was
about week before the tragedy. 1t was
at night about 8 o'clock. On cross-ex-
animation he testified that there was
space enough behind the door for per-
was opened to admit another person,
also that there were empty cartridge
shells in the slop jar upon his first visit
to the room, which was before Officer
Brady broke the pistol and took the
shells out. He testified that he had seen
Mrs. Bonine come out of the room OF





several single men, and her demeanor
was in no wise different from that when
he saw her emerge from Ayers room.


Thomas M. Baker an employe of the
Fish Commission who resided in the
building adjoining the Kenmore, was then
called and testified that on the night of
the tragedy he was awakened by the re-
ports of pistol shots. He jumped out of
the bed, went to the window and heard
u voice from above irquiring what was
wrong below. He replied that he had
heard pistol shots. Then, while standing
at his window, he saw figure on the
fire escape just outside of Ayres' window.
The figure walked the length of the fire
escape in his direction and then descend
ed two flights to the floor of the veranda
where it disappeared into a window. 1t
was the figure of small woman. clad
in dark tight fitting clothing. The wo-
man wore no hat, and as he did not hear
the fall of her footsteps he judged she
was in her stocking feet. He described
the manner of her descent, which he
said was very deliberate and without
emotion.


He did not know the defendant at the
time of the tragedy but saw her about
/ o'clock the afternoon of that day. She
was at that time being questioned by
Detective Horne. She was smiling and
he heard her say she knew nothing
about the cause of Ayres' death


Robert p. Hopkins, a clerk in the
War Department, heard three loud re-
ports and looking out saw something
which looked like a skull flying on the
fie escape just outside the window of
Ayre's room.


Emma A. LaWless, who occupied the
room adjoining that in which the trag-
edy occurred showed considerable ner-
vousness as she took the stand. She was
slightly aroused during the night of the
tragedy, but was not awakened. She
formed no idea as to what aroused her
or what time it was.


After the recess Miss Mary e. Minas.
a clerk in the Census Office, who occu-
pied the room next to Ayres' took the
stand. She testified that she was a
friend of Ayres.

Suggestions for the development of libraries in towns and small cities are summed up in the advice to write to the Office of the Student Volunteer Movement, No. 8 West Twenty-ninth street, New York City, which is particularly rich in knowledge of how to obtain libraries.

A club which, unlike most others in the list, meets actively only in summer is the Woman's Club of Chautauqua. The club is a department of the Chautauqua assembly and meets daily during the assembly, except Saturdays and Sundays. The sessions are held in the mornings, and consist of conferences, reading, study, and addresses on the lines of the work in which the club is interested. Education, household economics, social ethics, philanthropy, and art comprise its departments, and special topics in each of them are assigned for consideration at different meetings. As Chautauqua attracts specialists in many lines of work, it is possible to secure one to address the club. The broader knowledge of topics which is thus gained in the summer is carried widely throughout the succeeding club year by the 300 members of the organization. Mrs. H. Vincent of Greeley, Colo., is the president.

In general interest in domestic science work among the club women of Colorado has resulted in the creation of a department of domestic science in the State Federation. Mrs. T. Busey of Indiana is the chairman of the committee, whose charge it has been placed to us. In its first circular this committee recommends that the preliminary effort should be directed toward home improvement, and to this end urges the study of architecture and sanitation. Outside work, it is suggested, that both city and country make a persistent effort to introduce cooking and sewing in the public schools. Another move: the Literary Union of Portland, Ore., has just voted to increase the use of its domestic science department by appropriating some money recently given to the School Decoration committee for the setting up of a demonstration kitchen in the new manual training building of the city. Two of the club members are also members of the school board, and the interest in the subject is largely due to this fact. It is most impossible, indeed, to keep pace with the multiplication of domestic science schools, departments, and enterprises that are now fostered and developed by women's clubs. Yet it is only a few years since even the board subject of household economics met with resistance at the hands of club women, and domestic science was an almost unadopted topic. The change has come about because the meaning and importance of both subjects are much better understood. It is realized that no detriment to life or work can be derived from them.

The second joint issue of the annual reports of the Citizens Relief Association and the Associated Charities, embracing also extracts from the report of the Washington Sanitary Improvement Company, which was organized during the winter of 1896-97 as a subcommittee of the Citizens Relief Association, has been published.

The interesting feature of the publication is the statement of the principles and methods of the relief association and the Associated Charities. The Citizens Relief Association, it is stated, stands for material aims. It incurs no administrative expenses itself and therefore requires that all who apply for food, fuel or shoes from its fund shall be investigated by the Associated Charities.

Personal and Social.

The Associated Charities stands for personal and social service. It gives material aims from its own general funds, but strives to bring about adequate treatment of each needy individual family upon the basis of an adequate understanding of his needs and resources.

The methods of the Associated Charities are described in nine brief paragraphs as follows:

First, investigation—Prompt tactful inquiry is made by trained agents, who visit each applicant's home and, when needful, his previous employers, references and earlier residences.

Persons solicited for aims should request report by the Associated Charities before giving. Cards for thus referring applicants are provided free.

Second, immediate aid—Emergency relief is secured at once from the Citizens Relief or from the Golden Book Fund, in case of actual distress with no delay or "red tape."

Third, permanent betterment—An energetic effort is made to secure for each needy person exactly that kind and amount of material aid, of employment, corrective influence, opportunity, friendly counsel, social intercourse or gradual upbuilding which is needful for the permanent relief of his distress and the improvement of his life.

Cooperative System.

Fourth, co-operation—The cordial working of various charities, churches, relief agencies, schools and other philanthropies is brought about by (1) the division agents, who visit all these workers, enabling them to avoid working at cross purposes, and (2) by a central system of permanent case records, whereby duplication, overlapping and inadequacy are prevented and whereby if two or more helpers are interested in the same applicant, they are informed. If one helper begins this year to aid a family which was previously assisted by another organization, these records enable the new worker to profit by his predecessor's experience.

Fifth, friendly visitors—Unpaid workers are enlisted to serve as friendly visitors to one or two families only. A friendly visitor is asked to give no material aims. Instead, for example, he may secure odd jobs or steady work for the unemployed man of a needy family, or washings and sewing if the family's head be a woman; he may promote the regular school attendance of the family's children and the improvement of their home life; advice, encouragement and his own larger resourcefulness the visitor may lend to neglected people, together with that upbuilding which comes only from personal contact and the assurance that somebody cares.

Sixth, provident habits—Stamp savings have been introduced by the association. Division agents and volunteers make weekly rounds among the neediest homes, persuading their occupants to save nickels, dimes and quarters regularly in attractive stamp deposit books. This system leads many to lift themselves above the requirement of aims by laying by small sums toward future needs.

Special Work.

Seventh, direct benevolencies—A Golden Book is kept for accounts of subscriptions given by persons who wish to devote money directly and without administrative expense, to distressed families. Special appeals are also issued frequently for funds to supply an artificial limb, to establish transportation for dependents to places where care is assured, or for other special cases. The agents, resources and experience of the association are freely at the service of givers who wish to have their charities applied in special ways or to specified classes of need.

Eighth, officialism avoided—In each division an unpaid committee, representing the managers, friendly visitors and subscribers of the association, meets weekly to pass upon all cases investigated by the paid agent. This division committee is comparable to a council of physicians; it also prevents the organization from becoming superficial and careless or formal and case hardened in the treatment of needy people.

Serve as Central Stations.

Ninth, neighborhood centers—Seven offices are maintained, strategically placed, to serve as centers for such individual or organized social service as may be needed in the most neglected communities. The "Instructive Visiting Nurse Society," the "Flower Guild," the "Citizens Relief," the "Provident Fund Committee," medical dispensaries, church and school workers and many others use these offices as charitable clearing houses and centers for philanthropy.

Denver, Col. Sept. 6.—Mr. Abner McKinley, brother of the president, accompanied by his wife and two daughters, arrived in Denver today in the private car of President Trumbull, of the Colorado Midland and Southern railroad. No communication has been had with him since the news of the shooting of the president was received.

Washington, Sept. 5.—Mr. Bowen, associated with President Burn of the Pan-American exposition, has telegraphed the White House, that Dr. Rixey and two other physicians are with the president.

Washington, Sept. 5, 11 o'clock. Colonel Montgomery, the chief operator at the White House, received a message from a confidential but reliable source in Buffalo saying that the informant had learned that the president's wounds were not necessarily fatal, and that it is believed that he will live.

Buffalo, Sept. 5, 3.50 p. m.—At the home of John Nowaks, 40 Broadway, it was stated that Nieman came there last Saturday. He said that he was from Toledo and that he came to Buffalo to see the exposition. He was alone and had no visitors. His valise contained an empty revolver case and a few clothes.

Buffalo, Sept. 5, 8 p. m.—Colonel Michael has wired Secretary Hay that the surgeons will send him an official bulletin of the president's condition which is now considered serious.

Dublin, N. H., Sept. 6.—Secretary Hitchcock has been informed of the shooting of President McKinley by telegram from Washington. The message did not express an opinion as to the seriousness of the president's condition.

Buffalo, Sept. 6.—Just after the arrival of the president at Mr. Millburn's house, Mr. Millburn gave out a statement saying that while the president's condition was serious the wounds were not necessarily fatal. Dr. John Hammeter of Baltimore, a specialist on stomach troubles, saw the president. He stated that he did not believe the wound would prove fatal.

Burlington, VT, Sept. 5.—Vice President Fairbanks, started at once for Buffalo. To the Associated Press representative he said: "I am too shocked and grieved to express my feelings."

A few minutes, when a bulletin was handed him saying that President McKinley's wound was not fatal, the vice president sent word to the gathering:

"Like all our people and like the whole civilized world, you will rejoice to hear this good news."

Pittsburg, Sept. 5—When informed of the shooting of President McKinley, Gen. Knox said: "I cannot imagine how any living creature could harbor such a thought as to take the life of the president. I am shocked at the awful news that I cannot talk further."

Pittsburg, Sept. 6.—President Shaffer of the Amalgamated association, when told of the attempted assassination of President McKinley, said he was much shocked at the report and could say nothing of strike matters under the existing circumstances.

New York, Sept. 6, telephone message received here quotes Senator Hanna as saying: "The president will live."

Detroit, Sept. 6.—When ex-Secretary of War Alger heard of the shooting of President McKinley he broke down completely. With tears streaming down his face he said he was incapable of saying anything except that it was a dastardly outrage.

Buffalo, Sept. 5.—Dr. David T. Day, superintendent of buildings, left the hospital. The president's respiration is easy and pulse good.

At 6 o'clock the president was put under the influence of antiseptic and Dr. Parkee began probing for the bullet.

The prisoner is now locked up at police headquarters.

Soon after the shooting Nieman was asked why he shot the president and he said: "I am an anarchist and I did my duty."

Dublin, N. H., Sept. 6.—Secretary Hitchcock, who has been stopping at Mount Monadnock, tonight when informed of the tragedy at Buffalo, said: "I am horrified to make any expression whatever." He immediately prepared to leave for Buffalo.

Buckland, Maine, Sept. 6.—Hon. John, who has been passing his vacation at the Long homestead, two miles from this place, learned of the shooting of President McKinley tonight. He was deeply affected by the news, which came to him while he was at the village. He proceeded to his home at once, declaring that he was undecided about future plans on account of the suddenness of the news. The secretary positively refused to say anything for publication.

Buffalo, Sept. 5.—The would-be assassin is a Pole named Fred Nieman, 28 years old, stands five feet nine inches high, weighs 151 pounds, has dark brown hair, blue eyes, smooth face, regular features with prominent nose. He speaks very good English, and has claimed to come from Cleveland, Chicago and Detroit, but has told so many stories that his home is still a matter of conjecture and is not yet known whether he was born in this country or not. The district attorney is not conversant with him. All the police reserves have been called into the central office to guard against possible trouble and the police headquarters are flooded of block distant in each direction.

Denver, Sept. 6.—Abner McKinley, who with his wife and two daughters left here this morning for Bailey's in South Platte Canyon over the Colorado and Southern railway, was notified late this afternoon that the shooting of the president occurred. He started at once for Denver. He will reach here about 10 o'clock, and at 2 o'clock will leave for Chicago over the Burlington. He will travel to Buffalo over the Lake Shore, unless President McKinley dies before he reaches him.

The Squire was at the Tippers' and Tap Club last evening and received there reports of all of his men in all of the boroughs about the progress of the campaign. Although he told all inquirers he thought that his ticket would be elected. It was plain that every one of the men who were at the club was uneasy. I am more confident of the success of the ticket this evening than I have been at any time since the campaign began and he will win by a handsome majority, but I have no figures to give out at this time. We will carry Brooklyn and Manhattan. I have not given out the details of the canvasses on which our predictions are made. Why should I? If I did the enemy would concentrate all of their energies in the districts which we expect to carry tomorrow, and they would attempt to out down our vote.

Why should not Shepard run well in Kings county, he lives there. Brooklyn ought to give Mr. Shepard a very handsome majority. Brooklyn ought to be very proud of Mr. Shepard for the manner in which he has conducted his campaign. The people over there ought to be proud of him for the manner in which he has come out of all of his speeches for pure out-and-out Democracy. Mr. Shepard is one who would make a good Mayor, and there isn't any doubt that he will be elected Mayor.

What effect do you think the fusion charges of corruption, blackmail and bad administration will have on the campaign? Or that talk of the opposition about blackmailers and thugs being in a conspiracy and running the city is simply a part of the conspiracy among the Republicans to frighten the voters and the people. That is it. Have you gentlemen thought how long Tammany has been in power in New York during the last sixteen years. Prosperity has been brought about and in which all the great public improvements have been made.

Somebody figured out that Tammany had been in power about twelve years out.

That's right said Mr. Croker. Tammany's been in power all but about three years, and those were dead years. Now just consider the condition of our city to-day. All I have got to say is that if as though opposition claim blackmailers and thugs run the city, then I would recommend that a large number of cities in the United States be run in the same way. Every right-minded man knows that blackmailers and thugs and thieves couldn't run the city in a decent way, and they couldn't run it in the successful way in which New York has been managed.

Why, the other night a very prominent man told me he was going to vote the Tammany ticket for the first time in his life. He said that he had heard all this talk about the awful condition of New York, and that he made a personal investigation and that he was not able to find the conditions fusionists tell about. He said he didn't hear of any bank robbers, safe breaking, and thugs and highwaymen, like he used to, and he was going to vote for Tammany.

Then Mr. Croker told a story. It was the story of Lincoln and the critic who said that Gen. Grant drank too much whiskey, whereupon Lincoln said that if he knew the brand of whiskey he'd send some to certain other Generals.

That's a good parallel to the condition that exists here now, he said. Our opposition has been trying to blacken the name of the city. It has done it for partisan purposes. Isn't it strange that in spite of these attacks men of money come here to invest, to go into business, to build homes and bring up their families? and nine other anarchists under arrest
on the charge of conspiracy to assassi-

nate President McKinley, stand a good

Habeas corpus proceedings were be-

Chang and Taotai Shang, who hope
to escape censure by throwing the
blame for the transaction upon Ferguson.

WASHINGTON, Nov. 2. President
Roosevelt to-day issued his proclama-
ton, fixing Thursday, Nov. %, as day
of national Thanksgiving. It follows:
The season is nigh when, according to
the time-hallowed custom of our people,
the president appoints day as the
especial occasion for praise and thanks
giving to God.


This Thanksgiving finds the people
still bowed with sorrow for the death
OF great and good president. We
mourn President Mckinley because we
loved and honored him; and the man
ner Of his death should awaken in the
breasts of our people keen anxiety for
the country, and at the same time a
resolute purpose not to be driven by
any calamity from the path of strong,
orderly hopeful liberty. which as a
nation we have thus far safely trod.
Yet, in spite of this great disaster, it
is nevertheless true that no people on
earth have such abundant cause for
thanksgiving as we have. The past
year in particular has been one of
peace and plenty. We have prospered
in things material, and have been able
to work for our own uplifting in things
intellectual and spiritual. Let US re-
member that, as much has been given
US, much will be expected from US, and
that true homage comes from the heart
as we'll as from the lips, and shows
itself in deeds. We can best prove our
thankfulness to the Almighty by the
way in which, on this earth, and at this
time, each of US does his duty to his
fellow man.


Now, therefore, I, Theodore Roose-
welt, president of the United States, do
hereby designate as day of general
thanksgiving, Thursday, the 18th of
this present November, and do recon-
mend that throughout the land the
people cease from their wonted occupa-
tlons, and at their several homes and
places of worship reverently thank the
Giver of all Good, for the countless
blessings on our national life.


In witness whereof, I have here
unto set my hand, and caused the seal
of the United States to be affixed.


Done at the City of Washington,
this second day Of November, in the
year of our Lord one thousand nine
hundred and one, and of the Independ-
dence of the United States, the one
hundred and twenty sixth.


THEODORE ROOSEVELT.
By the President:


JOHN HAY, Secretary of State.

G. H. Vose of Kinebec has recently sold a fine gentleman's driver to S. W. East, New Portland. The horse was black with star in forehead, stood 16 hands and was won by Monitor Wilkes.

John G. Gibbons of Geneva, and J. Damon of Rochester, are the owners of the successful trotter Marla, driven by Young Jim, trained and driven by Geo. G. Hunt, of La Porte, Ind. She drove in 11 races the past season and won many of them.

G. H. Vose of Kinebec has bought the horse Geo. of S. S. Austin. He is one of the finest acting horses that has been around these parts, and Mr. Vose says he can go better than three minutes to a wagon. Geo. is a chestnut, weight about 1,100 pounds, and is an owned brother to Susie.

T. H. Greeley of Ellsworth has received a letter from R. T. Drake of Ohio harness, telling him something of two-year-old Lilly which he saw at the Lexington meeting recently. The filly is a full sister to Mr. Greeley's handsome bay, Leanitt. Mr. Drake writes that the filly was worked in spring and shipped to the Detroit meeting, where she was taken sick, shipped home and turned out. She was taken in again late in August, and two weeks ago was worked three miles in 5:08, 5:10, and 5:22 respectively. She went the last half of the last mile in 1:05, and the last quarter of the second mile in 32, Mr. Drake says she had kept well and would have beaten 3:00 this year. Naturally, all this is good news for Mr. Greeley, especially coming on, it does on top of the performance of Leanitt's half brothers at Sturbridge, Mass. last week. Until last week there were records for 1901. We're slow in putting in an approval early in the campaign, and hers were practically the only ones of the season. Snow behind him, over the 3:00 of Coney, made a harness, and over the 2:40 of Free Bond, that was an amateur performance and made without harness. The most important feature of the performance of Little Boy was the demonstration that next to Star Pointer he is trained almost entirely on the less important tracks. He never commanded the attention of the public that he deserved, and the opinion of the western critics who pronounced him the next two-minute pager, was taken with more than one grain of salt. Chickasha, I. T., May 17.—The secretary of the interior department, according to information from semi-official sources, has decided upon the location of the 100,000 acres of pasture lands in the Kiowa and Comanche country. The belief has prevailed that the entire tract would be located in the southern part of the reservation. The plans of Secretary Hitchcock are said to provide for locating 100,000 acres along Red River, the tract extending as far east as a north and south line through Fort Sill. This location will cover a greater part of Cache Creek and comprises some of the best lands in the entire reservation. South of the military timber reservation, which is practically west of Duncan, I. T., will be a tract of 10,000 acres, much of which is valuable agricultural land. South of the Kiowa hills, in the valley of the Little Washita river, will be another 10,000 acre tract which has been watched with hungry eyes by many farmers familiar with the country. Another tract is to be located south of Lone Wolf.


This plan is finding opposition among persons who are anxious to see the Indians given land only for grazing and who hoped that the fertile lands would fall to the homesteaders. Taking advantage of the mineral land clause of the act of Congress of 1900, settlers are already locating numerous agricultural claims in good localities. They stick their stakes for mineral locations, but they are really used as pretexts for being close to good land on the day of the opening.

fought the battle of Buena Vista, one
of the decisive conflicts of the Mexi-
can War.


General Zachary Taylor was in com-
mand at Buena Vista. The position
chosen by him was at the north end
of the valley known as Las Angostu-
ras, or the Narrows, and near the
hacienda or plantation known as
Buena Vista, from which the battle
took its name. The American forces
were disposed so as to secure every
advantage afforded by the lay of the
land, and the road through the pass
—the key to the whole position—was
swept by artillery. The troops were
in high spirits. It was Washington's
birthday, and this incident was com-
mented upon as being a good omen.


About noon a Mexican officer brought
a note to General Taylor, in which
Santa Anna demanded the surrender
of the American Army. This demand
was refused, but nothing definite was
accomplished that day.


During the night of the 22d, Santa
Anna reinforced the column under
Ampudia, and opened the battle at
daybreak on the 23d of February by
trying to turn the American left.
This attempt was successful, but the
attack upon the center was repulsed
by the Americans.


At this moment General Taylor arrived upon the field from Saltillo,
bringing with him May's Dragoons,
several companies of Mississippi rifle
men, and a portion of the Arkansas
cavalry, embracing every man that
could be spared from Saltillo. It was
a critical moment, for the turning of
the American left flank had neutraliz-
ed the advantage of the position.
Many of the troops were in retreat
upon Buena Vista, and nothing but
the courage of the remainder could
save the day. By great exertion, a
Colonel Jefferson Davis rallied the
greater part of his own regiment—the
Mississippi rifles—and part of the
Second Indiana, and by sharp ad-
vance drove the enemy from his front.
This had barely been accomplished
when thousands of Mexican lancers at-
tackled him. Forming his men into
letter V, with the opening towards the
enemy, Davis ordered them to await
the near approach of the enemy. He
had posted Sherman's battery on the
left, and the Mexicans galloped into
fire which could not be withstood.
They fled.


While this attack was going on, the
Mexicans sent a body of cavalry un-
der Torrejon to take the plantation of
Buena Vista. They were driven back
by the Kentucky and Arkansas volun-
teers, assisted by Colonel May's Dre-
goons. Colonel Yell of the Arkansas
regiment was killed and Torrejon
wounded in the engagement.


Santa Anna now sent a strong force
to the left in the effort to gain Tay-
lor's rear, and Torrejon's retreating
men joined their comrades. The
movement was detected by Colonel
May, who met the enemy. General
Taylor sent assistance in cavalry and
Bragg's Battery. Surrounded, the
5000 Mexicans seemed ready to sur-
render or be exterminated. In this
emergency the white flag was raised,
and parley asked for. The Ameri-
cans ceased firing, whereupon the
Mexican right escaped under the flag
of truce and joined the main army, at
the base of the mountain.


Santa Anna brought up his reserves,
and, with 4,000 men, rushed to at-
tack the Americans, who had been
fighting eight hours and who were out-
numbered nearly four to one. Tay-
lor's only hope was to concentrate his
scattered regiments. Bragg's artillery
was the first to arrive in re-enforce-
ment. Others of the Americans came
up rapidly. The Mexican right flank
was turned, and they broke and fled.

ers are ended she takes the water

bands grave.

water has a soothing effect on the
spirit Of the departed or not may ba
q matter Of conjecture, but. having
made it, the widow feels that she haa
done all that a be required Of her.
and enters wedlock again without mis-
giving.

The scene of the accident was a point about two miles out of Green Bush, on the line of the Albany and Hudson railway. The point where the cars met on the single track was at a sharp curve, and so fast were both running and so sudden was the collision that the motorman never had time to put on the brakes before southbound car No. 9 had gone almost clean through northbound car No. 11 and hung on the edge of a high bluff with its load of shrieking humanity. One motorman was killed instantly, while the other one lived but a few minutes.

Fully 100 men, women and children formed a struggling, shrieking pyramid, mixed with blood, detached portions of human bodies and the wreckage of the cars. Some of the more slightly injured of the men extricated themselves and began to pull people out of the rear ends of the two cars and almost every one was taken out in this way and nearly all were badly injured. This is a subject which should interest all classes of railroad men, especially those having heavy grades. We depend on the air brake for safety and fast time, so we should give it the necessary attention. Do not sacrifice a little time for inspection to insure safety. To the engineer I would say upon your good judgment and knowledge of the brake the greatest responsibility rests in getting your train safely over the road; therefore YOU should read all circulars issued by your company PERTAINING to air brakes carefully and live to them, as they AFFORD YOU means of protection and insure you from being cut out from any part of your train.

Before leaving any terminal point satisfy yourself that the air apparatus on your engine is in GOOD working order and do not wait until you are out on the road and break down. I will admit that a man may leave a terminal point with everything in good working order and break down a few miles out. These things will happen; they cannot be prevented, but there is no excuse for a man going out with air apparatus that is not capable of doing its work, and on arrival at destination failing to report any defective part.

The air pump is the manufacturer, and without a good pump it is impossible to do good WORK; therefore it should receive good attention. Do not abuse it. So that your lubricator is working correctly, don't dry the air cylinder with oil, and observe. Also don't run the pump too fast. I won't attempt to tell YOU how fast it should be run; your own judgment should govern YOU. On a train with perhaps a train of forty cars be sure that you have your excess pressure. Let your pump run at a moderate rate, not exceeding 100 strokes per minute, and let the inspector come over the train to take up the leaks in the train pipe and hose couplings. Upon signal from INSPECTOR to apply the brakes make a service application of fifteen rounds and at the same time under the length of train line exhaust.

The idea of a half round reduction is that, due to leaks in the train line the pressure can be retained longer in train pipe than if a twenty pound reduction was made, thereby giving the inspector chance to locate the same if he missed it on previous inspection. Also, a ten pound reduction with five or six inch standing piston travel is equal TO a full service application and will be sufficient for the inspector to make his adjustment of the brake. Do not infer from this that it would be full service while running if your piston travel varies from one TO two inches more while running, due to the wear of the journal bearings and the lost motion in the pedestals.

Keep the brake valve IN full release position at least ten seconds, and do not open the throttle immediately or you will break in two. You have already noted by the length of train line exhaust that it takes five or six seconds TO apply the brake on forty cars. It also takes that time for the pressure to get to the rear end OF the train and it takes as many more seconds for the brake TO release.

In starting down a heavy grade be sure that your auxiliaries are charged to seventy pounds, or seventy pounds and keep an eye on the air gauge. Don't lean your head out of the cab window in making the reduction as you may make your reduction too heavy and slow the train too suddenly. You will then have to release immediately and before you can recharge TO seventy pounds in the auxiliaries it will be necessary to apply the air brake. You are then braking with lesser power and instead of six or seven pounds reduction to steady the train, it will REQUIRE ten or twelve pounds. Don't wait until your train gets a start on you from twenty or thirty miles per hour; I contend that a seven or eight pound reduction running at the rate of eighteen or twenty miles per hour is equal to ten or twelve pounds reduction running thirty miles per hour.
